Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Reuters Massachusetts Judge tells jury in Lindsay Clancy trial to keep deliberating after deadlock Clancy does not deny strangling her three children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions Associated Press and Guardian staff Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.54 EDT First published on Tue 1 Sep 2026 10.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The judge has told the jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial to keep deliberating after it said it was unable to come to a unanimous decision in the controversial case of the mother who killed her three children. Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse in Massachusetts , does not deny strangling her children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. The jury could convict her of murder or manslaughter, or acquit her if jurors believe her deteriorating mental health was to blame. A conviction could lead to a life prison sentence. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation determines she is a danger to the public. Tuesday marked the fourth day of jury deliberations, which began after closing arguments on Thursday. Clancy’s lawyer argued at the trial that she loved her children, but killed them because she had lost her grip on reality – and on herself – due to postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth. In the months before the killings, Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital. Prosecutors said Clancy strangled the children because she was depressed and tired of living, and made a conscious choice to kill them before attempting suicide. To be found guilty, Massachusetts law requires defendants to retain “the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law”. Clancy’s former husband, Patrick, was among those to testify during the trial, in addition to relatives, psychologists and physicians who treated her. Jurors learned that Clancy had been prescribed 13 different sleep and anxiety medications, with her attorneys maintaining that may have exacerbated her depression symptoms. After Clancy’s criminal trial, the focus is going to shift to civil litigation brought by both Lindsay and Patrick against her medical and mental healthcare providers. The former couple accused the providers of medical malpractice, contending they failed to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her severe postpartum psychiatric condition. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images Waste Two more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in Oxfordshire A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m Charlie Moloney Tue 8 Sep 2026 17.54 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men have been arrested after fly-tippers dumped a “mountain of illegal waste”, stacked 10 metres high, in Oxfordshire . Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish appeared in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington in November last year. The waste tip was so large that removing it could cost more than the local council’s annual budget, the area’s MP said. The clean-up operation, which concluded last month, took five months. An estimated 22,704 tonnes of rubbish were cleared, with the operation costing an estimated £6m. The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed on Tuesday that a 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey had been arrested. It brings the total number of people apprehended to six, after one arrest in February, two in January and one in November, the EA said. The watchdog shut down the Kidlington site in October after officers discovered continued criminal activity after the first report of dumping at the site in July 2025. Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: “The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community. “We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation. These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington.” Dame Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said: “This government said we’d take on waste criminals and that’s exactly what we’re doing. “These arrests are another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste. “The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended. We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities.” The two men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations. The EA previously announced it was to spend millions of pounds to clear the enormous illegal rubbish dump, saying the waste was at risk of catching fire. Its policy is to refuse to clear up illegal waste dumps across the country, instead pursuing the perpetrators and landowners. But officials said they had taken the exceptional decision to clear up the waste outside Kidlington, which is next to the River Cherwell, because the scale of the fire risk set it apart from other illegal waste dumps in England and presented an overriding public imperative. The agency was given no extra money to clear the waste, and the EA said this would come from “making efficiencies in its operations”. The cost to the taxpayer would also include the payment of the landfill tax on the waste to the Treasury. The dumping in Kidlington took place under the noses of the EA, which was monitoring the site after being alerted to suspicious activity. During a meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Mr Burnham reiterated there would be âno change in the UKâs steadfast supportâ for Kyiv. He also urged Ukraineâs allies to send more interceptor missiles to Kyiv, and co-chaired his first coalition of the willing meeting, where he said the group was doing âeverything we canâ to âdig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocksâ. One of the last known times a CIA chief travelled to Russia was when Mr Ratcliffeâs predecessor William Burns held talks in the months ahead of the Kremlinâs full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The visit has sparked widespread speculation that it could be pre-empting new military action by Putin. Russiaâs aggression in Ukraine and rising hybrid activities against NATO allies leave no room for complacency. Latviaâs threat assessment remains unchanged. Together with our NATO allies, we are taking the necessary measures to strengthen our security. The Wall Street Journal, citing officials familiar with the visit, reported that he had visited to dissuade the Kremlin from attacking a NATO country. It added that US intelligence believes that Putin is considering testing the resolve of NATO with a limited assault which could include a cyberattack or a small-scale land invasion. The attack, it warns, would be on a Baltic country. Chairing his first meeting of the so-called âcoalition of the willingâ, the Prime Minister said the group was doing âeverything we canâ to âdig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocksâ. Mr Zelenskyy has repeatedly pleaded for more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles in recent months as Kyivâs stocks have diminished. Supplies of Patriots have been diverted to the Middle East since the outbreak of war with Iran, with Ukraine receiving significantly fewer missiles this year than in previous years. Speaking later on Monday, Mr Zelenskyy welcomed the talks between the coalition of the willing but said ânow, we have to deal with a funding gapâ, including the option of bringing forward part of the European loan to Ukraine, or unlocking frozen Russian assets. âThe total gap is 27 billion,â he said in a post on X. âOne of the main options is to bring forward part of the European loan funding this year. But we should not give up on other ideas for how to ensure fair protection in this war â a war that Russia started and continues to prolong.â Russia has sought to capitalise on the shortage by stepping up its ballistic missile strikes, killing at least 23 people and wounding more than 100 in the past three days alone. At a meeting of the coalition of the willing in Kyiv on Monday, Mr Burnham said the group was âworking with our allies outside of this coalitionâ to resolve the issue, arguing Ukraine âneeds more help to protect its people right nowâ. He also called on the US to âratchet upâ economic pressure on Russia, arguing Moscowâs economy was struggling under a record budget deficit and declining oil revenues and urging American legislators to impose further sanctions.
